lessons.title: Translate shapes on a grid
lessons.summary: Move every vertex by the same column vector, then describe or reverse the movement.
lessons.objective: Move every vertex by the same column vector, then describe or reverse the movement.
lessons.before: For Core and Extended. Be able to plot and read points on a coordinate grid.
lessons.ideas:
The top entry of a column vector is the horizontal movement. The lower entry is the vertical movement. Positive means right or up, and negative means left or down.

Choose matched points and compare their x-coordinates and y-coordinates from object to image.

To return to the original point, reverse the horizontal and the vertical movements.
lessons.method:
How do the two entries tell me where to go?

Move one vertex at a time, then join corresponding image vertices in the same order. A translation preserves the shape, size and orientation.

How do I find the vector from two corresponding points?

Subtract the old coordinate from the new coordinate in each direction. Check a second corresponding pair if both shapes are shown.

How can I undo a translation?

Subtract the original translation vector from the image coordinates. You can also translate by the vector with both signs changed.
mistakes: Read across first, then up or down. Swapping the two entries gives a different move.
Give the name of the transformation as well as the vector when asked to describe a translation fully.
Subtract a negative component carefully. It moves the point in the opposite direction.

examples.question: Triangle ABC has vertices \(A(1,-1),\quad B(3,-1),\quad C(2,2)\). Translate it by \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\6\end{pmatrix}\). Give all three image vertices.
examples.title: Translate a triangle
examples.solution:
The horizontal move is \(6\) and the vertical move is \(6\).

Make this same move from each vertex, then join the corresponding vertices in the original order.

The coordinates are \((7,5),\;(9,5),\;(8,8)\).

examples.question:
A single transformation takes triangle \(A(-2,-1),\quad B(1,-1),\quad C(-1,1)\) to \(A′(2,-9),\quad B′(5,-9),\quad C′(3,-7)\). Which description is correct?

  1. Translation by \(\begin{pmatrix}-4\\8\end{pmatrix}\).
  2. Translation by \(\begin{pmatrix}-8\\4\end{pmatrix}\).
  3. Reflection in the x-axis.
  4. Translation by \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\-8\end{pmatrix}\).
examples.title: Give a complete translation description
examples.solution:
The same directed move takes each original vertex to its image. That identifies a translation.

Each horizontal change is \(4\) and each vertical change is \(-8\).

examples.question: A translation by \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\-7\end{pmatrix}\) takes a point to \((-2,-7)\). Find the original point.
examples.title: Find the point before a translation
examples.solution:
Reverse both components of the movement. The reverse vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}-5\\7\end{pmatrix}\).

Apply that reverse movement to the image.

The coordinates are \((-7,0)\).

lessons.title: Reflect in horizontal and vertical lines
lessons.summary: Reflect points and shapes in axis-parallel mirrors and give the equation of the mirror line.
lessons.objective: Reflect points and shapes in axis-parallel mirrors and give the equation of the mirror line.
lessons.before: For Core and Extended. Be able to plot and read points on a coordinate grid.
lessons.ideas:
The mirror line lies halfway along the perpendicular segment from a point to its reflection.

Join a point to its image. The mirror passes through the midpoint of this segment and is perpendicular to it.

A point on the mirror has zero perpendicular distance from it. The point remains in exactly the same place after reflection.
lessons.method:
How do I use a mirror line on the grid?

For a vertical line, count horizontally to the mirror and continue the same number of units on the other side. For a horizontal line, count vertically.

How can I find the mirror line from an object and image?

When only x changes, the mirror is vertical and its equation starts with x. When only y changes, it is horizontal and its equation starts with y.

What if the vertex already lies on the mirror?

After reflecting each vertex, check lengths and orientation. The reflected image is the same size with its orientation reversed.
mistakes: Do not count along the mirror itself. Move at right angles to it.
Write a line such as x = 3 as an equation, using the coordinate that is fixed along the entire line.
A repeated vertex label can mark a point shared by object and image. Keep it in both shapes.

examples.question: Reflect triangle ABC with vertices \(A(3,3),\quad B(6,3),\quad C(4,7)\) in the line \(y=1\). Enter the three image vertices.
examples.title: Reflect a triangle in an axis-parallel line
examples.solution:
Measure the distance to the mirror line \(y=1\) along the perpendicular grid direction.

Place each corresponding image point the same distance from the line on the opposite side.

The coordinates are \((3,-1),\;(6,-1),\;(4,-5)\).

examples.question:
A reflection in a vertical line maps \((9,4)\) to \((1,4)\). Give the full description.

  1. Reflection in \(x=5\)
  2. Reflection in \(y=5\)
  3. Reflection in \(x=6\)
  4. Reflection in \(x=4\)
examples.title: Find the position of the mirror line
examples.solution:
Only the x-coordinate changes. The mirror is perpendicular to the segment joining the points.

The changing coordinate is halfway between its original and image values, giving \(x=5\).

examples.question: What is the image of \((7,4)\) under reflection in \(y=4\)?
examples.title: Recognise a point that stays fixed
examples.solution:
The point lies on the mirror line, so its perpendicular distance from the line is zero. It stays fixed.

The coordinates are \((7,4)\).

lessons.title: Rotate about the origin, a vertex or a midpoint
lessons.summary: Use quarter-turns and half-turns about Core centres and fully describe a rotation.
lessons.objective: Use quarter-turns and half-turns about Core centres and fully describe a rotation.
lessons.before: For Core and Extended. Be able to plot and read points on a coordinate grid.
lessons.ideas:
Find the centre and imagine an arm from it to a vertex. The arm changes direction by a quarter-turn and keeps the same length.

Locate the centre first. If it is a midpoint, mark it halfway between the two given vertices. Leave the centre in place.

A full description uses the name rotation, the centre, the angle and the direction when the directions differ.
lessons.method:
How do I make a quarter-turn on a grid?

Use tracing paper or count the relative steps from the centre. For an anticlockwise quarter-turn, an arm pointing right turns up. Check the sense before marking the image.

How do I rotate about a vertex or midpoint?

Rotate each relative movement from this centre. For a half-turn, the image lies the same distance on the opposite side of the centre.

What do I include in a full description?

Use a corresponding ray from the centre to compare its before and after directions. A \(180^\circ\) turn has the same result in either sense.
mistakes: Read the centre from the question. Turning round the origin gives a different image when the centre is elsewhere.
A centre can lie on an edge. It only stays in the same place itself, not the entire edge.
An angle without a centre does not specify one rotation.

examples.question: Triangle ABC has vertices \(A(-2,-4),\quad B(0,-4),\quad C(-1,-2)\). Rotate it through \(90^\circ\) clockwise about the origin \((0,0)\). Give the three image vertices.
examples.title: Rotate a shape about a stated centre
examples.solution:
For each vertex, count its horizontal and vertical steps from the centre of rotation.

Turn that relative movement through \(90^\circ\) clockwise and add the centre back. Join the rotated vertices.

The coordinates are \((-4,2),\;(-4,0),\;(-2,1)\).

examples.question: Triangle ABC has vertices \(A(2,-4),\quad B(8,-4),\quad C(4,4)\). Rotate it through \(90^\circ\) clockwise about the midpoint of AB \((5,-4)\). Give the three image vertices.
examples.title: Rotate a shape about a stated centre
examples.solution:
For each vertex, count its horizontal and vertical steps from the centre of rotation.

Turn that relative movement through \(90^\circ\) clockwise and add the centre back. Join the rotated vertices.

The coordinates are \((5,-1),\;(5,-7),\;(13,-3)\).

examples.question:
Triangle \(A(-1,-4),\quad B(1,-4),\quad C(0,-1)\) maps to \(A′(-1,-4),\quad B′(-3,-4),\quad C′(-2,-7)\) by a rotation. Which description is complete and correct?

  1. Rotation through \(180^\circ\) about \((-1,-4)\).
  2. Rotation through \(90^\circ\) clockwise about \((-1,-4)\).
  3. Rotation through \(180^\circ\) about \((1,-4)\).
  4. Rotation through \(180^\circ\) about \((0,-3)\).
examples.title: Describe the centre, angle and direction
examples.solution:
A and A′ are at the same point \((-1,-4)\). This point stays fixed.

The line from A to B turns through \(180^\circ\) to reach the line from A′ to B′.

lessons.title: Enlarge from a centre with a positive factor
lessons.summary: Draw larger and reduced images from a centre, and recover a positive scale factor or centre.
lessons.objective: Draw larger and reduced images from a centre, and recover a positive scale factor or centre.
lessons.before: For Core and Extended. Be able to plot and read points on a coordinate grid.
lessons.ideas:
The centre and each pair of corresponding vertices lie on one ray for a positive factor.

Compare two matching lengths, or compare the distances from the centre to an original point and its image.

Draw straight lines joining matched vertices, then extend them. The common meeting point is the centre of enlargement.
lessons.method:
How do I measure from the centre?

For example, a factor of \(2\) puts an image vertex twice as far from the centre. A factor of \(\frac12\) puts it halfway along the same ray.

How can I recover the scale factor?

Divide image length by object length. If the image is smaller, the positive factor is between zero and one.

How can I find a missing centre?

Use two non-parallel joins. Verify the same factor at a second vertex after locating the centre.
mistakes: Scale a vertex's displacement from the centre. Multiplying its absolute coordinates works only when the centre is the origin.
Dividing in the opposite order gives the factor for going back to the object.
The meeting point may be outside both shapes, so extend the joins far enough.

examples.question: Enlarge triangle ABC with vertices \(A(4,4),\quad B(10,4),\quad C(6,10)\) by scale factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) from centre \((0,2)\). Give the image vertices.
examples.title: Construct an enlargement
examples.solution:
Draw or imagine a line through the centre and each original point.

Multiply each displacement from the centre by \(\frac{1}{2}\). The image is on the same ray from the centre.

The coordinates are \((2,3),\;(5,3),\;(3,6)\).

examples.question: An enlargement with centre \((3,-1)\) maps \(A(9,1)\) to \(A'(12,2)\). Find the scale factor.
examples.title: Find an enlargement factor
examples.solution:
Find the horizontal moves from the centre to the object and from the centre to the image. The directions match.

Divide the image displacement by the object displacement.

The result is \(\frac{3}{2}\).

examples.question: One enlargement of scale factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) takes \(A(5,1),\quad B(11,1),\quad C(7,9)\) to \(A′(3,-2),\quad B′(6,-2),\quad C′(4,2)\). Find its centre.
examples.title: Locate the centre of an enlargement
examples.solution:
Join corresponding vertices, for example A to A′ and B to B′. The centre lies on both extended lines.

The lines meet at \((1,-5)\). Check that each image distance from this point has the stated scale factor.

The coordinates are \((1,-5)\).

lessons.title: Use diagonal mirrors, other centres and negative factors
lessons.summary: Extended: reflect in any straight mirror, rotate round a specified centre and interpret a negative scale factor.
lessons.objective: Extended: reflect in any straight mirror, rotate round a specified centre and interpret a negative scale factor.
lessons.before: For Extended. Recall how to read coordinates and directed movements on a grid.
lessons.ideas:
Use the perpendicular to the mirror through the vertex. Find the perpendicular foot, then continue the same distance beyond it.

Translate your thinking to the centre: compare each vertex with that centre, rather than with the origin of the whole grid.

The image moves to the opposite ray from the centre. The magnitude of the factor controls the size of the image.
lessons.method:
How do I reflect across a diagonal or oblique line?

For a diagonal on a square grid, the perpendicular is the other diagonal direction. For a general straight line, use a constructed right angle or a known perpendicular foot.

What if the rotation centre is outside the object?

Turn the relative movement by the stated angle, then start from the centre and make the new movement.

What changes when the scale factor is negative?

A factor of \(-\frac12\) means half the original distance away, on the opposite side. A factor of \(-2\) doubles the distance on that opposite ray.
mistakes: The horizontal distance is not the perpendicular distance for an oblique mirror.
The distance from the centre must be unchanged after any rotation.
Keep the sign in the description. The size alone cannot tell you which side of the centre the image is on.

examples.question: Reflect triangle ABC with vertices \(A(2,4),\quad B(4,4),\quad C(3,8)\) in \(y=-x+3\). Give its image vertices.
examples.title: Reflect in a diagonal mirror
examples.solution:
For each vertex, follow a perpendicular to \(y=-x+3\). For this diagonal, the perpendicular uses a slope of \(1\).

Carry that same perpendicular distance beyond the mirror to mark the new point. Repeat for all three vertices.

The coordinates are \((-1,1),\;(-1,-1),\;(-5,0)\).

examples.question: Triangle ABC has vertices \(A(-2,-4),\quad B(0,-4),\quad C(-1,-1)\). Rotate it through \(90^\circ\) clockwise about \((-6,-1)\). Give the three image vertices.
examples.title: Rotate a shape about a stated centre
examples.solution:
For each vertex, count its horizontal and vertical steps from the centre of rotation.

Turn that relative movement through \(90^\circ\) clockwise and add the centre back. Join the rotated vertices.

The coordinates are \((-9,-5),\;(-9,-7),\;(-6,-6)\).

examples.question: Enlarge triangle ABC with vertices \(A(1,5),\quad B(7,5),\quad C(3,13)\) by scale factor \(-\frac{3}{2}\) from centre \((-3,3)\). Give the image vertices.
examples.title: Construct an enlargement
examples.solution:
Draw or imagine a line through the centre and each original point.

Multiply each displacement from the centre by \(-\frac{3}{2}\). The image is on the opposite side of the centre.

The coordinates are \((-9,0),\;(-18,0),\;(-12,-12)\).

lessons.title: Apply and describe combined transformations
lessons.summary: Extended: keep track of the order of two steps and identify a single equivalent transformation where it exists.
lessons.objective: Extended: keep track of the order of two steps and identify a single equivalent transformation where it exists.
lessons.before: For Extended. Recall how to read coordinates and directed movements on a grid.
lessons.ideas:
The object for the second step is the image from the first step. A labelled intermediate figure makes it clear which points to move next.

Each reflection reverses the orientation. Two such reflections restore it. With parallel mirrors, the final movement is a translation.

Follow a point through the two steps and express the final coordinates in terms of the original ones. Compare that rule with a known transformation.
lessons.method:
Which shape goes into the second transformation?

Complete the stated first transformation and label its vertices. Apply the second one to those vertices, then give the final image.

What do two parallel reflections do?

Its component perpendicular to the mirrors is twice the signed separation from the first mirror to the second. Its parallel component is zero.

How can I check whether one step has the same effect?

Confirm that the same single rule works for the whole shape. Give the line, centre, factor, angle or vector required by that transformation.
mistakes: Swapping the steps can move the final image to a different position.
Use the difference between the mirror positions, with its sign. Reversing the reflections reverses the translation.
A single description has to be true for every vertex, not just the first one you checked.

examples.question: Triangle ABC has vertices \(A(-3,-3),\quad B(0,-3),\quad C(-2,-1)\). Reflect in \(x=-4\), then translate by \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). Give the final image vertices.
examples.title: Apply a reflection and translation in order
examples.solution:
Reflect the triangle in the stated line and label the intermediate vertices.

Translate that intermediate triangle. The order matters because the horizontal move appears in a different place relative to the reflection.

The coordinates are \((0,-6),\;(-3,-6),\;(-1,-4)\).

examples.question: Reflect a shape in \(x=-6\), then reflect its image in \(x=0\). The two steps give one translation. Find its column vector.
examples.title: Find the single movement from two parallel reflections
examples.solution:
A point with x-coordinate \(x\) first changes to \(2(-6)-x\).

The second reflection changes this to \(2(0)-[2(-6)-x]=x+12\). Its y-coordinate has not changed.

The column vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\0\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.question:
A shape is reflected in \(x=0\) and then translated by \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\0\end{pmatrix}\). Which single transformation has the same effect?

  1. Reflection in \(x=-2\)
  2. Reflection in \(x=4\)
  3. Translation by \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\0\end{pmatrix}\)
  4. Reflection in \(x=2\)
examples.title: Recognise a single equivalent transformation
examples.solution:
The x-coordinate changes from \(x\) to \(2(0)-x+4\) and y stays unchanged.

Rewrite the x rule as \(2(2)-x\). Its fixed x-value is \(2\), the new mirror line.

lessons.title: Add, subtract and scale vectors
lessons.summary: Extended: read directed displacements, combine column vectors and multiply every component by a scalar.
lessons.objective: Extended: read directed displacements, combine column vectors and multiply every component by a scalar.
lessons.before: For Extended. Recall how to read coordinates and directed movements on a grid.
lessons.ideas:
The first letter of \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) is the start and the second is the end. Its components are obtained from end minus start.

To add, put the tail of the next arrow at the head of the first. The resultant goes directly from the original start to the final end.

A scalar multiplies both components. A positive scalar keeps the direction. A negative scalar points in the opposite direction.
lessons.method:
What changes if I reverse the arrow?

Reversing the arrow changes the signs of both components and keeps the length.

How do I add or subtract two vectors?

Add matching components. To subtract a vector, reverse both of its signs and add the reversed vector.

What does a scalar do to a vector?

Apply any scalars first, then add or subtract the resulting components. State the complete column vector.
mistakes: A vector describes a movement, so it can be drawn from a different starting point without changing its components.
Do not cross the components or reverse only one sign when subtracting.
A negative scalar does not change just the vertical direction. It reverses the whole vector.

examples.question: Given \(A(-1,8)\) and \(B(-5,15)\), find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) as a column vector.
examples.title: Read a directed line as a column vector
examples.solution:
Start at A and travel to B. Subtract the coordinates of A from those of B.

The column vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}-4\\7\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.question: Given \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}9\\-4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\8\end{pmatrix}\), calculate \(\mathbf a-\mathbf b\).
examples.title: Add or subtract matching components
examples.solution:
Work with the two horizontal components together. Then work with the two vertical components.

When subtracting, reverse both components of the second vector before adding.

The column vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}14\\-12\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.question: Given \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-4\end{pmatrix}\), find \(-2\mathbf a\).
examples.title: Multiply both components by a scalar
examples.solution:
Multiply the horizontal and vertical components by the same scalar.

A negative scalar reverses the vector and also changes its length when its magnitude is not one.

The column vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}-12\\8\end{pmatrix}\).

lessons.title: Find vector magnitudes
lessons.summary: Extended: use perpendicular components to find a vector length, including exact roots and a missing component.
lessons.objective: Extended: use perpendicular components to find a vector length, including exact roots and a missing component.
lessons.before: For Extended. Recall how to read coordinates and directed movements on a grid.
lessons.ideas:
The horizontal and vertical components are perpendicular. Pythagoras gives \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) for the magnitude.

First find the directed displacement by subtracting the starting position from the final position. Then apply Pythagoras to the two resulting components.

Square the given length and take away the square of the known component. The result is the square of the unknown component.
lessons.method:
Why do I square the components?

Square each signed component with brackets, add the squares, then take the non-negative square root.

How do I find the magnitude between two points?

Replacing a vector by a negative multiple can reverse its direction. Its length scales by the absolute value of that multiple.

How can I recover a missing component?

Use the required sign to choose a square root when the question states a direction or sign.
mistakes: Adding component lengths gives an L-shaped route. The magnitude is the length of the direct movement.
A vector can have negative components. A magnitude cannot be negative.
The given magnitude is already a length. Square it before using it in the inverse calculation.

examples.question: A vector has column form \(\begin{pmatrix}-10\\-4\end{pmatrix}\). Find its exact magnitude.
examples.title: Use Pythagoras for the magnitude
examples.solution:
The horizontal and vertical components form perpendicular legs. Square both signed components and add the squares to get \(116\).

Take the non-negative square root of the sum.

The result is \(2\sqrt{29}\).

examples.question: Given \(P(-5,-1)\) and \(Q(13,2)\), work out \(|\overrightarrow{PQ}|\) exactly.
examples.title: Find the length of a directed line segment
examples.solution:
Subtract the coordinates of P from those of Q to get \(\begin{pmatrix}18\\3\end{pmatrix}\).

Square the two components, add, then take the positive square root.

The result is \(3\sqrt{37}\).

examples.question: The vector \(\begin{pmatrix}-15\\t\end{pmatrix}\) has magnitude \(\sqrt{229}\). Given \(t>0\), find \(t\).
examples.title: Find a missing component from the magnitude
examples.solution:
Square the stated magnitude to get \(229\). The first component contributes \(225\).

So \(t^2=229-225=4\). The positive value is required.

The result is \(2\).

lessons.title: Use position vectors, routes and ratios
lessons.summary: Extended: use arrows through the origin and express midpoints and internal divisions in terms of two vector directions.
lessons.objective: Extended: use arrows through the origin and express midpoints and internal divisions in terms of two vector directions.
lessons.before: For Extended. Recall how to read coordinates and directed movements on a grid.
lessons.ideas:
A position vector always starts at the origin. A displacement between two points starts at the named first point and may not touch the origin.

Follow a known route and add its movements. Reverse the sign of any vector used in the opposite direction.

An internal ratio counts parts on both sides of the point. Add the two numbers to find the total parts.
lessons.method:
Which arrows start at the origin?

Use end position minus start position. This combines the backwards journey to the origin with the forward journey to the end point.

How do I write a route using two directions?

If \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b\), then \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf a\).

What part of the full segment do I travel?

To get a position vector, reach the first endpoint from the origin and then travel the required fraction of the full segment.
mistakes: The named endpoint and the displacement can have different components even though they finish at the same point.
Changing the order of the letters changes the sign of the displacement.
A ratio such as 2 : 3 gives two fifths from the first end. It does not give two thirds of the full segment.

examples.question: Points S, T and U have position vectors \(\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\end{pmatrix}\), \(\begin{pmatrix}-5\\6\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\13\end{pmatrix}\) respectively. Find the directed displacement \(\overrightarrow{SU}\).
examples.title: Distinguish a position from a displacement
examples.solution:
A position vector starts at the origin. The displacement starts at S, so subtract the position of S from the position of U.

The column vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\12\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.question: In triangle OAB, \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b\). Start at A, go to O, then to B. Express \(14\overrightarrow{AB}\) in terms of \(\mathbf a\) and \(\mathbf b\).
examples.title: Use a route through the origin
examples.solution:
The journey to O is the reverse of the position vector of A.

Add the position vector of B and scale the whole displacement by 14.

The vector is \(-14\mathbf{a}+14\mathbf{b}\).

examples.question: In triangle OAB, \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b\). M divides AB internally with \(AM:MB=3:3\). Find \(\overrightarrow{OM}\) in terms of \(\mathbf a,\mathbf b\).
examples.title: Write the position vector of an internal point
examples.solution:
The full segment has 6 equal ratio parts. So \(\overrightarrow{AM}=\frac{1}{2}\overrightarrow{AB}\).

Start at O, travel to A, then add \(\frac{1}{2}\) of \(\mathbf b-\mathbf a\). Collect the coefficients.

The vector is \(\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}+\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{b}\).

lessons.title: Prove parallel, collinear and similar relationships
lessons.summary: Extended: use a scalar multiple and a shared point, recover ratios and compare the corresponding sides of similar triangles.
lessons.objective: Extended: use a scalar multiple and a shared point, recover ratios and compare the corresponding sides of similar triangles.
lessons.before: For Extended. Recall how to read coordinates and directed movements on a grid.
lessons.ideas:
Two nonzero vectors are parallel when one is a scalar multiple of the other. The scalar may be positive or negative.

Parallel directions can belong to different lines. To show that three points lie on one line, use two displacements with a common endpoint.

When two rays from a common vertex are scaled by the same positive factor, the new triangle is an enlargement of the old one.
lessons.method:
How can I show that two vectors are parallel?

Find a multiplier from one nonzero component, then check it scales the other component too. For an expression in two independent vectors, compare both coefficients.

What extra step proves that points are collinear?

For example, show that AC is a scalar multiple of AB and note that the two segments meet at A. The scalar can also locate C along that line.

How do I link a scalar and triangle similarity?

Subtract the two new position vectors to find the third side. Its scalar relationship to the old side gives the direction and the length ratio.
mistakes: Matching a single component is insufficient. Check the entire vector relationship.
When using a ratio, check where the point lies. A fraction between zero and one puts it between the endpoints.
Use corresponding sides in the same order. Reversing one arrow introduces a minus sign.

examples.question: Given \(\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-8\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-16\end{pmatrix}\), find the scalar \(k\) for which \(\mathbf v=k\mathbf u\).
examples.title: Show how two vectors are parallel
examples.solution:
Divide the horizontal component of v by the horizontal component of u.

Check the vertical components give the same multiplier. The two vectors are parallel because both components scale by that number.

The result is \(2\).

examples.question:
Let \(A(3,-9),\quad B(15,-17),\quad C(21,-21)\). The vectors \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AC}\) share the starting point A. Which reason shows that A, B and C lie on one line?

  1. The points are collinear because \(\overrightarrow{AC}=\frac{3}{2}\overrightarrow{AB}\) and both start at A.
  2. The points are collinear because \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{AC}\).
  3. The points are collinear because two of them have the same x-coordinate.
  4. The points cannot be collinear because the two displacements differ in length.
examples.title: Check the scalar multiple and the common point
examples.solution:
End minus start gives \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}12\\-8\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}18\\-12\end{pmatrix}\).

The second vector is \(\frac{3}{2}\) times the first. They share A, so A, B and C are on one straight line.

examples.question: In triangle OAB, \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b\). P lies on OA and Q lies on OB, with \(\frac{OP}{OA}=\frac{OQ}{OB}=\frac{9}{23}\). Express \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\) in terms of \(\mathbf a,\mathbf b\).
examples.title: Relate corresponding sides of similar triangles
examples.solution:
The two position vectors are \(\frac{9}{23}\mathbf a\) and \(\frac{9}{23}\mathbf b\). Use end minus start.

The result is \(\frac{9}{23}\) times \(\overrightarrow{AB}\). The corresponding sides are parallel and the triangles are similar.

The vector is \(-\frac{9}{23}\mathbf{a}+\frac{9}{23}\mathbf{b}\).

questions.title: Translate a triangle
questions.prompt_html: Triangle ABC has vertices \(A(0,4),\quad B(2,4),\quad C(1,6)\). Translate it by \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\5\end{pmatrix}\). Give all three image vertices.
questions.solution_html:
The horizontal move is \(5\) and the vertical move is \(5\).

1. Enlarge triangle ABC with vertices \(A(2,4),\quad B(8,4),\quad C(4,10)\) by scale factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) from centre \((-2,2)\). Give the image vertices.

    [2]

  2. An enlargement with centre \((4,4)\) maps \(A(7,6)\) to \(A'(10,8)\). Find the scale factor.

    [2]

  3. A single transformation maps \(A(8,3),\quad B(14,3),\quad C(10,9)\) to \(A′(5,1),\quad B′(8,1),\quad C′(6,4)\). Describe the transformation fully.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Draw or imagine a line through the centre and each original point.

Multiply each displacement from the centre by \(\frac{1}{2}\). The image is on the same ray from the centre.

The coordinates are \((0,3),\;(3,3),\;(1,6)\).

(b)

Find the horizontal moves from the centre to the object and from the centre to the image. The directions match.

Divide the image displacement by the object displacement.

The result is \(2\).

(c)

The shape keeps its angles but the side lengths change in a common ratio. The transformation is an enlargement.

The ratio of matching side lengths is \(\frac{1}{2}\). The extended joins of corresponding vertices meet at \((2,-1)\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Scale the displacement from the centre. Add the centre back after scaling.

(b)

The scale factor is the image distance divided by the original distance.

(c)

Find the scale from related sides and the centre from lines through two corresponding pairs.

marking_criteria.description_html: Scale each displacement from the given centre, keeping track of which side of the centre the image lies on.
Compare the image distance from the centre with the corresponding object distance.
Use a common side-length ratio and the intersection of the vertex joins to describe the transformation.
Enlargement with centre \((2,-1)\) and scale factor \(\frac{1}{2}\).

questions.title: Reflect in a diagonal mirror
questions.prompt_html: Reflect triangle ABC with vertices \(A(-2,-2),\quad B(0,-2),\quad C(-1,2)\) in \(y=-x\). Give its image vertices.
questions.solution_html:
For each vertex, follow a perpendicular to \(y=-x\). For this diagonal, the perpendicular uses a slope of \(1\).

Carry that same perpendicular distance beyond the mirror to mark the new point. Repeat for all three vertices.

The coordinates are \((2,2),\;(2,0),\;(-2,1)\).
questions.hint_html: Count along diagonals perpendicular to the mirror, not along horizontal rows.

questions.title: Use the perpendicular foot to reflect across a line
questions.prompt_html: The perpendicular from \(P(5,10)\) to the mirror line \(2x+3y=14\) meets the line at \(M(1,4)\). Find the reflection of P.
questions.solution_html:
The mirror passes through the midpoint of the segment joining P to its image.

Repeat the directed movement from P to M once from M. This puts the image the same distance beyond \(M\) along the perpendicular.

The coordinates are \((-3,-2)\).
questions.hint_html: The foot M is halfway along the segment from P to its reflection.

questions.title: Compare two similar triangles
questions.prompt_html:
1. In triangle OAB, \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b\). P lies on OA and Q lies on OB, with \(\frac{OP}{OA}=\frac{OQ}{OB}=\frac{11}{17}\). Express \(\overrightarrow{PQ}\) in terms of \(\mathbf a,\mathbf b\).

    [2]

  2. In triangle OAB, \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b\). Point M has position vector \(\overrightarrow{OM}=\frac{2}{7}\mathbf{a}+\frac{5}{7}\mathbf{b}\). Find the simplified ratio AM : MB and show why M lies between A and B.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The two position vectors are \(\frac{11}{17}\mathbf a\) and \(\frac{11}{17}\mathbf b\). Use end minus start.

The result is \(\frac{11}{17}\) times \(\overrightarrow{AB}\). The corresponding sides are parallel and the triangles are similar.

The vector is \(-\frac{11}{17}\mathbf{a}+\frac{11}{17}\mathbf{b}\).

(b)

Subtract the position vector of A. Then \(\overrightarrow{AM}=\frac{5}{7}(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\).

This is a positive fraction of AB less than one, so M lies between A and B. Compare that starting fraction with the rest of the segment.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Find OP and OQ first. The vector PQ is OQ minus OP.

(b)

Find AM first by subtracting the position of A.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the given common fraction on both position vectors, then subtract the first position from the second.
\(-\frac{11}{17}\mathbf{a}+\frac{11}{17}\mathbf{b}\)
Use AM as a scalar multiple of AB and compare the travelled fraction with what remains.
